title_hi: Financial ROI in AI Architecture Build vs Buy Framework for Financial Operations
summary: Evaluating generative AI as infrastructure requires a structured build-versus-buy framework to calculate accurate Total
content:
Evaluating generative AI as infrastructure requires a structured build-versus-buy framework to calculate accurate Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) and maximize financial ROI.


  
  
  The Cost of AI Infrastructure


Financial executives must evaluate generative AI not as software, but as infrastructure. The true cost extends beyond API tokens to include data pipelines, vector storage, and continuous model evaluation. A structured build-versus-buy framework clarifies these hidden expenses and aligns AI deployment with financial return on investment (ROI).


  
  
  Build vs Buy Framework


The decision to build custom models or buy API access hinges on data sensitivity and latency requirements. Buying access through providers like OpenAI or Anthropic minimizes upfront capital expenditure (CapEx) and accelerates time-to-market. Building custom infrastructure using open-source models (like LLaMA) increases CapEx but stabilizes operational expenditure (OpEx) for high-volume inference.


  
  
  Total Cost of Ownership Calculation


Calculate the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) by projecting token usage over 24 months. Compare this against the cost of renting GPU instances (e.g., A100 or H100) and hiring specialized ML engineers. For most financial operations, buying API access yields a higher ROI during the first year, while building becomes cost-effective only when inference volume exceeds the break-even threshold of 500 million tokens per month.


  
  
  Strategic Implementation


Implement AI capabilities iteratively. Start with API-based services to validate use cases and measure ROI. Once a workflow proves profitable and token volume scales, transition to self-hosted open-source models. This hybrid approach limits financial risk while building internal engineering capability.

content:
Как составить proposal for freelancers, который закрывает сделку, а не лежит в папке «Отправлено»


Если вы фрилансер, знакомо это чувство: лид тёплый, вы обсудили задачу, клиент говорит «звучит отлично, пришлите коммерческое». Вы садитесь вечером писать предложение, тратите три часа, отправляете — и тишина. Через неделю узнаёте, что клиент ушёл к другому подрядчику, который просто ответил быстрее и понятнее.

Проблема почти никогда не в цене. Проблема в том, что proposal for freelancers часто пишется как эссе о вашей крутости, а не как документ, который помогает клиенту принять решение. Ниже — разбор структуры, конкретные формулировки и чек-лист, который можно применить к следующему проекту уже сегодня.


  
  
  Почему большинство предложений не срабатывают


Три типичные ошибки:



Слишком долго. Пока вы «шлифуете» документ два дня, клиент уже подписал кого-то другого. Скорость ответа — конкурентное преимущество.

Слишком абстрактно. «Комплексный подход к разработке», «креативные решения под ваш бизнес» — это не информация, а шум.

Нет границ. Не описано, что входит в работу, а что нет. Потом начинаются бесконечные правки, и проект становится убыточным.


Хороший proposal решает одну задачу: снимает неопределённость. Клиент должен за 5 минут понять, что вы делаете, сколько это стоит, когда будет готово и что от него требуется.


  
  
  Структура proposal, которая работает


Вот каркас из 7 блоков. Порядок важен — он ведёт клиента от «понимаю проблему» к «готов подписать».


  
  
  1. Заголовок с сутью, а не с вашим именем


Плохо: «Коммерческое предложение от Ивана Петрова».
Хорошо: «Ре дизайн лендинга для SaaS-продукта: сроки, объём и стоимость».

Клиент сканирует список писем. Заголовок должен напоминать, о чём была речь, и обещать конкретику.


  
  
  2. Понимание задачи (2–4 предложения)


Повторите задачу словами клиента. Это доказывает, что вы слушали, и защищает от недопонимания.

Пример:
> Вы запускаете новую версию продукта и хотите, чтобы лендинг конвертировал холодный трафик из рекламы. Сейчас страница не отражает новое позиционирование, а форма заявки теряет лиды на мобильных.

Здесь же — одна-две метрики успеха, если клиент их озвучил (рост заявок, снижение отказов, срок запуска).


  
  
  3. Что именно вы сделаете


Разбейте на этапы с конкретными действиями. Не «дизайн сайта», а:


Аудит текущей страницы и 3 конкурентов
Прототип в Figma (десктоп + мобильная версия)
Дизайн 1 экрана в 2 вариантах на выбор
Финальный макет с UI-китом
Передача в вёрстку с комментариями


Каждый пункт — это то, за что клиент платит. Чем конкретнее, тем меньше вопросов на созвоне.


  
  
  4. Что НЕ входит в работу


Этот блок многие пропускают, а он спасает от 80% конфликтов. Перечислите честно:


Копирайтинг текстов (если не входит)
Вёрстка и подключение к CMS
Закупка фото и лицензий
Правки после утверждения финального макета


Формулировка «не входит» не отпугивает клиентов — она показывает, что вы профессионал, который считает своё время.


  
  
  5. Сроки и этапы


Таблица или список с датами или длительностью:




Этап
Длительность
Что нужно от вас




Аудит и прототип
3 дня
Доступ к аналитике


Дизайн
5 дней
Фидбек в течение 24 часов


Финальная передача
2 дня
—




Обратите внимание на колонку «что нужно от вас» — она мягко перекладывает часть ответственности за сроки на клиента.


  
  
  6. Стоимость и условия


Варианты подачи цены:



Фикс за проект — если объём понятен.

Фикс + почасовые доработки — если возможны изменения.

Разбивка по этапам — снижает порог входа для клиента.


Обязательно укажите: предоплату (обычно 30–50%), количество раундов правок, что считается «правкой», а что «новой задачей».


  
  
  7. Следующий шаг


Один конкретный призыв. Не «жду вашего ответа», а:

> Если всё ок — ответьте «согласен», и я пришлю договор и счёт на предоплату. Старт возможен с понедельника.

Чем меньше шагов до старта, тем выше конверсия.


  
  
  Чек-лист перед отправкой


Пройдитесь по пунктам — это займёт 2 минуты:


[ ] В заголовке есть суть проекта, а не только ваше имя
[ ] Задача сформулирована словами клиента
[ ] Список работ разбит на конкретные действия
[ ] Есть блок «что не входит»
[ ] Указаны сроки и что требуется от клиента
[ ] Прописаны условия оплаты и правок
[ ] Есть один чёткий следующий шаг
[ ] Документ читается за 5 минут
[ ] Отправлен в PDF или по ссылке (не .docx, который поедет вёрсткой)



  
  
  Как ускорить процесс до 30 минут


Главная причина, по которой фрилансеры тратят на proposal полдня, — каждый раз писать с нуля. Решение: шаблоны и переиспользуемые блоки.

Что стоит подготовить заранее:



Шаблон структуры — те самые 7 блоков выше.

Библиотеку формулировок — типовые блоки «что входит» для ваших услуг, типовые условия оплаты, типовые сроки.

Калькулятор цены — чтобы не считать в голове на созвоне.

Скрипты писем — для отправки, для фоллоу-апа через 3 дня, для ответа на «дорого».


Когда всё это лежит в одном месте, вы заполняете пробелы под конкретный проект, а не изобретаете документ заново. Именно на это рассчитан «Freelance Proposal & Scope Kit: Close Deals in 30 Minutes» — набор готовых шаблонов предложений, чек-лист по объёму работ, калькуляторы цены и скрипты писем для дизайнеров, разработчиков и копирайтеров-одиночек. Если вы устали каждый раз собирать предложение вручную, это разумная точка старта за $19.


  
  
  Частые вопросы


Сколько страниц должен быть proposal?
Для большинства фриланс-проектов — 2–4 страницы. Всё, что длиннее, читают редко. Если проект крупный, лучше сделать короткое резюме на первой странице и детали — дальше.

Что делать, если клиент просит «просто цену»?
Дайте цену — но с одной строкой объёма: «Дизайн лендинга, 5 экранов, 10 дней — $X». Это защищает от ситуации, когда под «просто ценой» клиент подразумевал совсем другой объём.

Как отвечать на «дорого»?
Не снижайте цену сразу. Спросите: «С чем сравниваете?» Часто выясняется, что клиент сравнивает с другим объёмом работ. Тогда предложите урезанную версию — без потери ставки.

Нужен ли договор, если есть proposal?
Proposal фиксирует ожидания, договор — обязательства. Для проектов дороже нескольких сотен долларов лучше и то, и другое. Многие пункты из proposal можно перенести в договор как есть.


  
  
  Что делать прямо сейчас

title: How to write a freelance proposal

How to Write a Freelance Proposal That Wins the Project (Step-by-Step)

You found a promising lead. You had a good call.
content:
How to Write a Freelance Proposal That Wins the Project (Step-by-Step)

You found a promising lead. You had a good call. Now you need to send a proposal — and this is where many freelancers either freeze or spend three days polishing a document that never gets signed.

The truth: clients don't hire the most beautiful proposal. They hire the one that makes the decision easy. A good proposal answers three questions fast: What exactly will I get? What does it cost? What happens next?

This guide walks you through how to write a freelance proposal step by step, with concrete structure, examples, and a checklist you can reuse for every project.





  
  
  Step 1: Start With the Client's Words, Not Your Bio


Most proposals open with "About me" and a list of tools. That's backwards. The client already knows they need help — they want to see that you understood the problem.

Do this instead:


Write a 3–5 sentence "Understanding" section that restates their goal in your own words.
Pull 1–2 direct quotes from your call or email.


Example:
> "You mentioned your SaaS blog gets traffic but almost no demo signups, and you want to publish two in-depth posts per month starting in March. You also want the tone to match your existing onboarding emails."

This single paragraph does more to build trust than a page of awards.





  
  
  Step 2: Define the Deliverables With Painful Specificity


Vague deliverables cause scope creep. "Website redesign" means nothing. "5-page marketing site redesign" is better, but still loose.

A strong deliverables list includes:



Quantity — how many of each item

Format — Figma file, Google Doc, WordPress draft, etc.

Length/size — word count, page count, screen count

Revisions — how many rounds, and what counts as a revision

What's excluded — this is the part most freelancers skip


Example (copywriter):


4 blog posts, 1,200–1,500 words each
2 rounds of revisions per post
SEO keyword provided by client

Not included: original photography, paid keyword research, CMS upload


The "not included" line prevents 80% of awkward conversations later.





  
  
  Step 3: Show the Process in 3–5 Steps


Clients feel safer when they can picture the workflow. Keep it short:



Kickoff call (30 min) — goals, references, access

Draft 1 delivered within X days

Feedback round — consolidated comments in one doc

Final delivery — files handed off with source assets

Optional: 14-day post-launch support


This also subtly signals you're organized, which justifies higher rates.





  
  
  Step 4: Price With Options, Not a Single Number


A single price invites a yes/no decision. Three tiers invite a which one decision — and that's a much easier conversation.

A simple structure:



Essential — core deliverables only

Standard — core + one high-value add-on (e.g., extra revision round, strategy call)

Premium — everything + ongoing support or priority turnaround


Keep the middle option as your recommended one. Most clients pick it.

Pricing tips:


Anchor with a project total, not hourly (unless the client demands hourly).
State deposit terms: e.g., 50% upfront, 50% on delivery.
Add a line for late-payment interest if you work with businesses.






  
  
  Step 5: Make the Next Step Obvious


End with a clear call to action. Not "Let me know your thoughts!" but:

> "If this looks good, reply 'approved' and I'll send the contract and invoice for the 50% deposit. I can start on [date]."

One action. One sentence. No ambiguity.





  
  
  Step 6: Keep It Under 2 Pages (Yes, Really)


Long proposals feel thorough to the writer and exhausting to the reader. Aim for:


1 page for small projects (under $2k)
2 pages max for larger ones
A separate scope document if things get complex


If you need more space, use an appendix — don't bloat the main pitch.





  
  
  Common Freelance Proposal Mistakes




No clear scope → endless revisions

Burying the price on page 4 → client loses interest

Too many options (5+ tiers) → decision paralysis

No expiration date → client sits on it for a month

Generic template → reads like it was sent to 10 other people


Add an expiration: "This quote is valid for 14 days." It's a small nudge that works.





  
  
  A Quick Pre-Send Checklist


Before you hit send, verify:


[ ] Client's name and company spelled correctly
[ ] Their goal restated in the first paragraph
[ ] Deliverables have quantity, format, and revision limits
[ ] Exclusions are listed
[ ] Timeline with specific dates
[ ] Price with deposit terms
[ ] One clear next step
[ ] Expiration date included
[ ] PDF exported (not a Google Doc link that might change)






  
  
  How to Write a Freelance Proposal Faster


Writing a great proposal once takes an hour. Writing it from scratch every time takes days you're not billing for.

The smart move: build a reusable system. Save your best-performing sections — the understanding paragraph, deliverables list, process, pricing tiers — and swap in project-specific details. What used to take an afternoon takes 30 minutes.

If you'd rather skip the setup work entirely, «Freelance Proposal & Scope Kit: Close Deals in 30 Minutes» is a $19 toolkit built exactly for this: fill-in-the-blank proposal templates, a scope checklist to prevent creep, pricing calculators, and email scripts for following up with leads until they sign. It's made for solo designers, developers, and copywriters who'd rather spend time on client work than on paperwork.





  
  
  Final Thought


A freelance proposal isn't a sales pitch — it's a decision-making tool. The faster a client can say yes, the more projects you close. Nail the structure, cut the fluff, and make the next step obvious.

Then send it, follow up in 3 days, and move on to the next lead.

title: How Python's venv Works — Why It Keeps Projects From Fighting Over the System Python
title_hi: How Python's venv Works — Why It Keeps Projects From Fighting Over the System Python
summary: Anyone who has worked with Python tooling has run into "virtual environments" (venv) sooner or later. A single command,
content:
Anyone who has worked with Python tooling has run into "virtual environments" (venv) sooner or later. A single command, python3 -m venv .venv, creates a directory that most Python projects treat as a given. What is that directory actually doing, and why has it become such a standard part of the workflow? This post looks at the problem venv solves and how it works under the hood.


  
  
  The Problem: Projects Sharing One Python Installation


Working on multiple Python projects on the same machine eventually runs into a conflict: one project needs version 2 of a library, another needs version 3 of the same library. Running pip install directly against the system Python installs into one shared site-packages directory for the entire machine, so installing the second project's dependencies overwrites the first project's, and one of them breaks.


Note: site-packages is the directory where third-party libraries installed via pip install actually live. Python looks inside it whenever code does an import.


On some operating systems, the system Python is also used internally by OS-level tooling (package managers, for instance), so carelessly installing or upgrading libraries into that shared location risks affecting the OS itself, not just your own projects. A virtual environment sidesteps this by giving each project its own independent site-packages, rather than everyone sharing one pool.


  
  
  What Actually Happens Inside a venv


Running python3 -m venv .venv creates a directory roughly structured like this:



.venv/
├── bin/                       # python3/pip executables (symlink or copy)
├── lib/.../site-packages/     # this project's own library directory
├── pyvenv.cfg                 # records where the base system Python lives






The key detail is that .venv/bin/python3 isn't a separate Python implementation — it's the same interpreter as the system Python, either copied or symlinked. What changes is where it looks for libraries. When .venv/bin/python3 starts up, it reads pyvenv.cfg and redirects its site-packages search path to .venv/lib/.../site-packages instead of the system-wide location. Any pip install run through that interpreter installs into this project-local directory, leaving the system Python's environment untouched.

The familiar source .venv/bin/activate command isn't the mechanism that provides this isolation — it's a convenience shell script layered on top. Running it just prepends .venv/bin to the PATH environment variable and sets a VIRTUAL_ENV variable, so that typing python or pip in the terminal afterward resolves to the venv's copies first. The isolation itself doesn't require activation at all: calling .venv/bin/python3 script.py by its full path gets you the same isolated environment, activated or not.


  
  
  A Real Example: Startup-Time venv Management in _launcher.sh


This app's Mac/Linux launch script, _launcher.sh, relies on exactly that direct, activation-free call for a health check:



if [ ! -f ".venv/bin/python3" ]; then
    NEEDS_SETUP=1
elif [ ! -f "$STAMP" ] || [ "$(cat $STAMP)" != "${ARCH}:${PY_VER}:${REQ_HASH}" ]; then
    NEEDS_SETUP=1
elif ! .venv/bin/python3 -c "import sys; sys.exit(0)" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    NEEDS_SETUP=1
fi






Rather than rebuilding .venv on every launch, the script keeps a stamp file at .venv/.install_stamp containing three values as a single string: the machine architecture (uname -m), the Python version, and a hash of requirements.txt. On the next launch, it compares this composite key against the stored one. If they match, .venv is assumed unchanged and reused as-is — the script just runs source .venv/bin/activate and moves on. If any of the three has changed (a dependency bump shipped in an app update, or the machine changing from Intel to Apple Silicon, for example), .venv is deleted entirely and rebuilt from scratch with python3 -m venv .venv followed by pip install -r requirements.txt.

The line .venv/bin/python3 -c "import sys; sys.exit(0)" looks like it does nothing, but it's a health check confirming the venv's Python binary can actually run. This can fail, for example, after an OS update moves the system Python's location out from under a symlink the venv still points to — in which case a rebuild is triggered as well.

This "don't rebuild unless the requirements.txt hash changes" design carries a hidden assumption worth naming. As covered in our post on pip's version-specifier syntax, this app's own requirements.txt uses >= lower-bound specifiers (like flask>=3.0.0) rather than == exact pins. That means the file's hash can stay identical across two separate pip install runs, while the actual library versions installed can still differ depending on when the install happened. A matching hash guarantees the venv was built from the same requirements.txt, not that its installed contents are byte-for-byte identical every time — a distinction worth keeping in mind.


  
  
  Summary


A venv solves the problem of multiple projects fighting over one shared Python installation by giving each project its own isolated site-packages. activate is a convenience layer that temporarily rewrites PATH; the actual isolation works by simply calling .venv/bin/python3 directly. This app's launcher script leans on that property, checking for environment drift (architecture, Python version, dependency changes) via a hash-based stamp file instead of rebuilding the environment on every single launch — while still catching the cases where it genuinely needs to.

content:
Menavigasi Tech Stack Modern di Tahun 2026: Antara Efisiensi dan Hype




Beberapa tahun terakhir, dunia pengembangan perangkat lunak terasa seperti perlombaan senjata. Setiap minggu ada framework baru, library state management baru, atau pendekatan arsitektur yang diklaim sebagai "penyelesai segala masalah". Namun, memasuki tahun 2026, ada pergeseran paradigma yang cukup terasa. Kita tidak lagi berada di fase "menambah alat baru", melainkan fase "konsolidasi".

Tren saat ini bukan lagi tentang siapa yang menggunakan tool paling banyak, tapi siapa yang bisa membangun sistem yang stabil dengan jumlah tool paling minimal.


  
  
  Konsolidasi di Sisi Frontend: React 19 dan Melampauinya


React masih mendominasi, namun cara kita menggunakannya telah berubah. Hadirnya React Compiler di versi 19 adalah titik balik yang signifikan. Masalah klasik seperti useMemo dan useCallback yang seringkali membingungkan pengembang junior—dan terkadang bahkan senior—kini mulai teratasi secara otomatis. Kita bisa kembali fokus pada logika bisnis daripada pusing memikirkan kapan komponen harus render ulang.

Next.js 16 juga membawa angin segar dengan Turbopack yang sudah matang, membuat siklus pengembangan terasa jauh lebih instan. Tapi menariknya, saya melihat banyak tim mulai melirik SvelteKit atau Astro untuk proyek yang lebih spesifik. Astro, dengan arsitektur islands-nya, menjadi pilihan utama untuk situs yang mengutamakan SEO dan kecepatan load, sementara SvelteKit memberikan pengalaman developer (DX) yang jauh lebih ringkas bagi tim kecil yang ingin bergerak cepat tanpa beban boilerplate yang berat.


  
  
  Backend: Go vs Node.js dalam Perang Efisiensi


Di sisi server, perdebatan antara Node.js dan Golang masih berlanjut, namun batasannya kini lebih jelas. Node.js dengan TypeScript tetap menjadi pilihan paling rasional untuk tim yang ingin satu bahasa di seluruh stack. Kecepatan iterasi yang ditawarkan sangat sulit dikalahkan, terutama dengan framework seperti Fastify yang kini jauh lebih efisien dibandingkan Express.

Namun, untuk layanan yang membutuhkan throughput tinggi atau sistem yang sangat terdistribusi, Go (Golang) telah menjadi standar industri. Kemampuannya dalam menangani konkurensi melalui goroutines membuat Go sangat superior untuk membangun API gateway atau microservices yang harus melayani jutaan request per detik dengan konsumsi memori yang minimal.

Bagi saya, pilihan terbaik saat ini adalah pendekatan hybrid: gunakan Node.js untuk lapisan API yang sering berubah dan membutuhkan integrasi cepat, lalu pindahkan logika berat atau service yang bottleneck ke Go.


  
  
  PostgreSQL: Satu Database untuk Segalanya


Jika ada satu tool yang benar-benar menang dalam hal konsolidasi, itu adalah PostgreSQL. Dulu kita mungkin merasa perlu MongoDB untuk data dokumen, Redis untuk caching, dan database vektor terpisah untuk AI. Sekarang, PostgreSQL dengan ekstensi seperti pgvector telah mengubah permainan.

Kita bisa menyimpan data relasional, JSONB untuk fleksibilitas dokumen, dan vektor untuk pencarian semantik AI dalam satu tempat. Ini mengurangi kompleksitas infrastruktur secara drastis. Tidak ada lagi drama sinkronisasi data antar database yang berbeda atau biaya operasional yang membengkak hanya untuk menjaga lima jenis database tetap hidup.


  
  
  AI dalam Workflow: Bukan Lagi Sekadar Copilot


Cara kita menulis kode juga telah berevolusi. AI bukan lagi sekadar alat untuk melengkapi baris kode (autocomplete), melainkan partner dalam berpikir. Tool seperti Cursor atau Claude Code memungkinkan kita melakukan refactoring skala besar atau migrasi codebase hanya dengan instruksi tingkat tinggi, asalkan kita paham arsitekturnya.

Namun, ada jebakan di sini. Banyak pengembang mulai terlalu bergantung pada AI sehingga melewatkan pemahaman fundamental. Di tahun 2026, nilai seorang engineer bukan lagi terletak pada kemampuan menulis sintaks—karena AI bisa melakukannya—melainkan pada kemampuan mendesain sistem (System Design), memastikan keamanan, dan melakukan debugging pada masalah-masalah edge case yang tidak dipahami oleh model bahasa besar.


  
  
  Kondisi Market dan Mentalitas Baru


Kondisi pasar kerja IT saat ini menuntut apa yang saya sebut sebagai "T-Shaped Developer". Perusahaan tidak lagi mencari seseorang yang "hanya bisa React" atau "hanya bisa Go". Mereka mencari engineer yang punya spesialisasi mendalam di satu bidang, namun memiliki pemahaman luas tentang bagaimana seluruh sistem bekerja—mulai dari CSS di browser, optimasi query di database, hingga konfigurasi CI/CD di cloud.

Kesimpulannya, teknologi akan terus berkembang, tapi fundamental tetap sama. Fokuslah pada pemecahan masalah, bukan pada tool-nya. Pilihlah stack yang memungkinkan Anda mengirimkan nilai ke pengguna secepat mungkin dengan risiko kegagalan sekecil mungkin.

Menurut kalian, apakah konsolidasi stack ini akan membuat kita menjadi developer yang lebih produktif, atau justru membatasi inovasi karena kita terlalu nyaman dengan tool yang itu-itu saja?

title: Zero-capital automation: running a business from Termux
title_hi: Zero-capital automation: running a business from Termux
summary:
Zero-Capital Automation: Running a Business from Termux


Okay, let's be real. The dream of starting a business
content:
Zero-Capital Automation: Running a Business from Termux


Okay, let's be real. The dream of starting a business often comes with a hefty price tag: office space, employees, marketing budgets… it can be paralyzing. But what if I told you you could bootstrap a surprisingly capable business, powered by automation, all from the terminal on your phone? Sounds crazy? Maybe. But I’m doing it, and this article will show you how.

I’m running a small data aggregation and alert service – FractalMesh – that monitors specific cryptocurrency price action and sends alerts via Telegram. It’s not making me a millionaire (yet!), but it’s self-funded, largely automated, and runs almost entirely from Termux on my Android phone.  And the best part? The initial investment was essentially zero.

What is Termux?

For those unfamiliar, Termux is an Android terminal emulator and Linux environment. It allows you to run a full Linux distribution (albeit a limited one) directly on your phone.  Think of it as having a mini-server in your pocket.  You can install packages with pkg, write scripts, and even run full-blown web servers.

Why Termux for Business?



Cost: Free. Seriously.

Portability: Your business is literally in your pocket.

Low Overhead: No need for expensive servers initially.

Privacy:  You control your data.

Learning Opportunity: Forces you to understand the fundamentals of system administration and automation.


The Tech Stack: A Minimalist Approach

My setup revolves around these core components:



Termux: The foundation.

Python 3: The scripting language of choice. Versatile, readable, and tons of libraries.

requests library: For fetching data from APIs (like KuCoin, Binance, etc.).

schedule library:  For scheduling tasks – crucial for automation.

python-telegram-bot library:  For sending alerts via Telegram.

jq:  A lightweight and flexible command-line JSON processor (install via pkg install jq).

Text Editor (Nano/Vim):  For writing and editing scripts directly on the phone.

Tmux (optional but highly recommended): A terminal multiplexer.  Allows you to run multiple terminal sessions within Termux, detach them, and reattach later – perfect for long-running scripts. Install via pkg install tmux.


The Core Logic: Python & Scheduling

The heart of my operation is a Python script that periodically checks cryptocurrency prices, compares them to pre-defined thresholds, and sends Telegram alerts if necessary. 

Here’s a simplified example:



import requests
import schedule
import time
import telegram

# Replace with your Telegram bot token
TOKEN = "YOUR_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN"
CHAT_ID = "YOUR_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID"

def check_kucoin_price(symbol):
    try:
        url = f"https://api.kucoin.com/api/v1/ticker/price?symbol={symbol}"
        response = requests.get(url)
        response.raise_for_status() # Raise HTTPError for bad responses (4xx or 5xx)
        data = response.json()
        price = float(data['data']['price'])

        if symbol == "BTC-USDT":
            threshold = 28000
        elif symbol == "ETH-USDT":
            threshold = 1700
        else:
            threshold = 0 # Default to no alert

        if price < threshold:
            message = f"🚨 ALERT: {symbol} price is below ${threshold}! Current Price: ${price}"
            bot = telegram.Bot(token=TOKEN)
            bot.sendMessage(chat_id=CHAT_ID, text=message)
            print(f"Alert sent for {symbol} at {price}")

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        print(f"Error fetching data for {symbol}: {e}")
    except KeyError:
        print(f"Error parsing JSON for {symbol}")



schedule.every(5).minutes.do(check_kucoin_price, symbol="BTC-USDT")
schedule.every(5).minutes.do(check_kucoin_price, symbol="ETH-USDT")


while True:
    schedule.run_pending()
    time.sleep(1)






Explanation:



Imports: Necessary libraries.

TOKEN & CHAT_ID:  Important: Replace these placeholders with your actual Telegram bot token and chat ID.  (See below for setup instructions).

check_kucoin_price(symbol): This function fetches the current price of a given cryptocurrency pair from the KuCoin API. It checks if the price falls below a predefined threshold and sends a Telegram alert if it does.  Error handling is included to catch network issues and API changes.

schedule:  The schedule library allows you to schedule the check_kucoin_price function to run every 5 minutes for both BTC and ETH.

while True loop: Continuously runs the scheduler.


Telegram Bot Setup



Talk to BotFather: In Telegram, search for "BotFather".

Create a New Bot: Use the /newbot command and follow the instructions. BotFather will provide you with a token.  Keep this secure!

Get Chat ID: Send a message to your newly created bot. Then, use a tool like https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates (replace <YOUR_TOKEN> with your bot token) in your browser. The JSON response will contain your chat_id.


Running It All in Termux



Install Python: pkg install python


Install required libraries: pip install requests schedule python-telegram-bot


Create the Python script:  Use Nano (nano your_script.py) or Vim (vim your_script.py) to create and save the script above.

Run the script: python your_script.py



Keeping It Running (Tmux to the Rescue!)

Simply running the script in Termux won’t work if you close the app or your phone goes to sleep. This is where Tmux comes in.



Start a Tmux session: tmux new -s my_session


Run your script inside the Tmux session: python your_script.py


Detach from the session: Press Ctrl+b, then d.

Secure by Design: The New Standard for DeFi

The landscape of decentralized finance has shifted dramatically. In 2026, r
content:
Secure by Design: The New Standard for DeFi

The landscape of decentralized finance has shifted dramatically. In 2026, relying solely on manual code review for smart contract audits is no longer viable. The complexity of cross-chain interactions and dynamic oracle data demands a hybrid approach where human expertise guides AI-driven analysis. Using AI for smart contract audits is no longer a futuristic concept; it is an operational necessity that reduces false positives and uncovers subtle logic bugs that traditional static analysis tools miss.

The core advantage of AI in this context is contextual understanding. Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on billions of lines of Solidity and Vyper code can interpret intent, not just syntax. For instance, an AI agent can identify that a reentrancy vulnerability exists not because of a specific pattern, but because the order of operations violates the "checks-effects-interactions" principle in a specific business logic context.

To implement this, developers are moving away from simple prompt-and-response workflows toward agentic pipelines. Consider this Python snippet using a hypothetical 2026 AI audit SDK:



from ai_audit_sdk import AuditAgent, ContextLoader

def run_ai_audit(contract_source_path, protocol_spec_md):
    # Load both the code and the natural language specification
    context = ContextLoader.load(
        code_file=contract_source_path,
        spec_file=protocol_spec_md
    )

    # Initialize an agent specialized in financial logic
    agent = AuditAgent(model="audit-v5-pro", mode="deep_reasoning")

    # The AI cross-references code logic with the spec
    # to find deviations that might indicate bugs
    findings = agent.analyze(
        context, 
        focus=["reentrancy", "oracle_manipulation", "access_control"]
    )

    return findings.generate_report(format="markdown")






Practical tips for maximizing this workflow involve "spec-first" auditing. Before deploying the AI, ensure your protocol specification is detailed and unambiguous. If the spec says "users can withdraw at any time," but the code has a lock period, the AI will flag this as a potential logic error. Without the spec, the AI might assume the lock is intentional.

Furthermore, use AI for regression testing. After fixing a bug, feed the diff to the AI along with the original vulnerability report. The model can verify if the fix introduces new edge cases

title: Your coding agent is only trustworthy where you can inspect its work. Draw that line.
title_hi: Your coding agent is only trustworthy where you can inspect its work. Draw that line.
summary: The October 6 Stack Overflow developer survey has a number that settles an argument I keep having on Tuesday afternoons:
content:
The October 6 Stack Overflow developer survey has a number that settles an argument I keep having on Tuesday afternoons:



Write code with AI where you can check the result fast.
Pull AI back where checking is expensive.






That is not a slogan. It is the survey compressed into one rule. Here are the numbers.



67%  use AI to generate code in areas they already know well
61%  use AI to debug
20%  use AI for production: deploy, operate, troubleshoot
78.7% say knowing the source matters to whether they trust an answer
6.6% trust AI for important decisions
48%  trust AI only when they can verify it themselves






Read the top and bottom together. Adoption is not the story. The boundary is the story. Developers trust an agent exactly as far as they can inspect its work.


  
  
  The 20% ceiling is the useful number


The 67% figure gets all the attention. The 20% figure is the one that should drive your design.

Generating code in a domain you already know has a property AI does not need to supply: you can see the error when the output is wrong. Debugging is the same. If the agent suggests a bad hypothesis, you test it and find out.

Production is different. Deploying, operating, and troubleshooting live infrastructure has a failure cost that dwarfs the cost of a bad diff. When the failure is in front of users, the check is not cheap. So developers keep AI out of the high-stakes end of the pipe. That is not technophobia. It is a risk-adjusted decision, and the survey shows developers have arrived at it empirically.


  
  
  Trust scales with inspectability


The survey's most useful split is not between AI users and non-users. It is between tasks where the developer can evaluate the output and tasks where they cannot.

That split is the rule you should encode. Concretely, it becomes a question you ask about every agent task before you let it merge anything:



Can I verify this output faster than I could have written it myself?







Yes: let the agent run. Tests, linters, and quick local reads make checking cheap.
No: pull the agent back. The task needs a human who can explain the change at 3 a.m.


This is the same question that separates your 67% tasks from your 20% tasks. The 20% is not a moral failure of the agent. It is a structural property of the task.


  
  
  A concrete example of the boundary


Take a refactor that renames a function and updates every call site. The agent can do that in one pass. Skip the phrasing noise; read the diff yourself. The check is: does the renamed symbol appear everywhere it should, and nowhere it should not? A compiler or test run answers that in seconds. This task sits on the 67% side of the line. Let the agent run.

Now take a migration that touches how your payment flow reads a stored value. The failure mode is not a compile error. It is a business decision: which value is authoritative, and who depended on the old one? A human who knows the domain has to read the change and say whether it is right. No test run decides that. This task sits on the 20% side. Pull the agent back.

The two tasks look similar on the surface. Both are code changes. The difference is whether a machine can run the check, or a person has to. That is the whole rule.


  
  
  Why the boundary is not about skill


It is tempting to read the survey as "senior developers trust AI less." The data does not support that reading. The split is by task, not by person. The same developer uses AI on the rename and keeps it away from the migration. That is not inconsistency. It is the boundary working.

What that means for a team is useful: you do not have to convince people to trust AI. You have to make the cheap-to-check work easy to verify, and make the expensive-to-check work hard to merge without a human. The trust follows the design, not the personality.


  
  
  The reviewer signal the survey gives you


The survey quietly contains a hiring signal. If your team's pull requests are full of changes nobody can explain, the 20% ceiling is telling you something. It is not that the agent is bad. It is that the work you are letting it touch has no cheap check, and you have not assigned a human who owns the merge.

The fix is structural: for every agent-touched branch, name the person who can explain it at 3 a.m. before the agent starts, not after the review fails. That single step moves the trust decision from "does the output look right" to "who is accountable for this working."


  
  
  Why source attribution is a design input, not a courtesy


The survey says 78.7% of developers want to know where an AI answer came from. Treat that as a functional requirement, not a preference.

When the model cites a function signature that does not exist, or an API shape it invented, the single most useful debugging fact is where the claim came from. Without provenance you cannot tell a real API from a hallucinated one. With it, you can.

So the practical step is: require every agent-generated code block to carry its source, or design the harness so the model must quote the API it is calling. That turns the 78.7% from a statistic into a per-merge checkpoint.


  
  
  The policy lag is where the real risk lives


The survey has one number that is easy to miss: only 24% of companies have published an approved AI toolset or a formal AI policy. The other 76% are letting individual developers make the call.

That is not a small gap. It means the trust boundary is being drawn per engineer, per pull request, with no shared rule. Two developers on the same team can reach opposite answers on the same task. The engineering fix is the same as for the code: make the boundary explicit and shared instead of implicit and personal.


  
  
  A workflow rule instead of a feeling


The whole survey, compressed into an enforceable line:



Before an agent writes to a shared branch:
1. Decide where the check is cheap. That is where the agent runs.
2. Decide where the check is expensive. That is where a human owns the merge.
3. Record the source of any claim you cannot verify from memory.






You can ship this as a lint rule, a pull-request template, or a paragraph in your contributing guide. The form matters less than the fact that it exists.


  
  
  Where I am unsure


I have not measured this on my own team. The 67%, 20%, and 6.6% figures are single-vendor survey numbers, published as percentages with no confidence interval. Treat them as direction, not precision.

What I am confident about is the structure: adoption and trust moved in opposite directions in this survey, and the split between inspectable and uninspectable work is the line that explains both. That structure has survived across every article in this space I have read this week.


  
  
  Sources



Stack Overflow 2026 Developer Survey, published October 6, 2026, 30,903 responses across 169 countries. Data and commentary via the survey report and secondary coverage (ComputerWeekly, CompareTheCloud, TechBuzz, Debugged-Pro citing CNN).
Adoption/trust figures are a single primary source (Stack Overflow) confirmed across multiple secondary reports.

title: Obsidian + Claude Code: The Shared Memory Stack I Actually Use
title_hi: Obsidian + Claude Code: The Shared Memory Stack I Actually Use
summary:
My notes used to be where ideas went to die.

Obsidian was my beautiful, over-organized graveyard. Claude Code was my br
content:
My notes used to be where ideas went to die.

Obsidian was my beautiful, over-organized graveyard. Claude Code was my brilliant intern who forgot everything after every shift.

Then I wired them together and stopped taking notes entirely. My stack started taking them for me.

This is not another "second brain" aesthetic post. This is the duct-taped, actually-working memory system that runs my dev life.


  
  
  The problem: two brains, zero memory


Here is what was happening before:

Obsidian knew everything I had thought. Old meeting notes, half-baked ideas, that snippet from 2022 I swear I would need later. Local, fast, mine. But dumb. It couldn't do anything.

Claude Code could do everything I wanted. Write code, refactor, ship features, run tests. But it had the memory of a goldfish on espresso. Every new session was "Hi, who are you and what is this codebase?"

I was the human API between them. Copying context from Obsidian into Claude. Copying what Claude did back into Obsidian. I was a very expensive clipboard.

So I stopped being the clipboard.


  
  
  The stack: stupidly simple


Three pieces. No vector database, no fancy SaaS, no $20/month AI wrapper that will die in 6 months.

1. Obsidian Vault as the Source of Truth
My vault lives at ~/vault. It's just Markdown. No database, no lock-in. Structure:



/00-inbox/           -> auto-fetched stuff lands here
/01-projects/        -> active builds, each with a CLAUDE.md
/02-memory/          -> the Memory Tree - people, decisions, bugs
/03-docs/            -> docs Claude actually reads






2. Claude Code with CLAUDE.md
Every project has a CLAUDE.md that Claude reads on startup. It's not a prompt. It's the operating manual.

Mine looks like this:



# Project: numbpilled-api
- Stack: Bun + Hono + Postgres
- Never run rm -rf, always use trash-cli
- Before coding, read /02-memory/decisions.md
- After coding, append what you did to /00-inbox/changelog.md






3. The Glue: A 20-line script that syncs them
Claude Code writes to Markdown. Obsidian reads Markdown. That's it. That's the integration.

I have a hook that runs after every Claude session:

echo "- $(date): $CLAUDE_TASK - files: $FILES_CHANGED - lesson: $LEARNED" >> ~/vault/00-inbox/changelog.md

No TokenJuice. No embeddings. Just files.


  
  
  How it actually works in real life


Morning:
I open Obsidian. In 00-inbox there is already a summary from last night. Claude finished the auth refactor at 11pm, wrote what it changed, what broke, what it learned. I didn't ask it to. It just does because CLAUDE.md told it to.

During work:
I don't prompt Claude with "here is the context." I prompt it with "read /02-memory/decisions.md and fix the billing bug like we did last time."

It knows. Because it wrote that file last week.

Example workflow that feels like cheating:

I say: /clear then "implement rate limiting, same pattern as the other routes"

Claude does this, without me pasting anything:


Opens 02-memory/patterns/rate-limiting.md - which it created
Reads the existing implementation
Applies it to the new route
Writes a new entry: 03-docs/rate-limiting.md - added to /api/numbpilled, limit 100/min



My Obsidian graph now has a new node. I did not make it.

The magic moment:
Last Tuesday I searched Obsidian for "why did we choose Hono over Express?" The answer was there. Not written by me. Written by Claude three weeks ago after I asked it to compare frameworks. It had appended its reasoning to 02-memory/decisions.md.

My AI remembered why I made a decision better than I did.


  
  
  Why this beats every "AI second brain" tool


Most tools try to be smart. This stack tries to be inspectable.


It's just files. If Claude hallucinates, I open the Markdown and delete the line. No black-box vector DB to re-index.
It compounds. Every session makes the next one smarter. My CLAUDE.md files are getting better without me editing them. Claude improves its own manual.
It works offline. My vault is local. My memory is local. When the API is down, I still have my brain.
It kills context switching. I live in Obsidian. Claude lives in the terminal. They meet in the middle as Markdown. I never copy-paste between them anymore.


I used to spend 6 hours a week on "knowledge management." Now I spend zero. The system manages itself.


  
  
  The setup, if you want to steal it


Day 1 - Make Claude write your memory:
Create ~/vault/02-memory/decisions.md and add this to your CLAUDE.md:

After every significant task, append 2-3 bullets to ~/vault/02-memory/decisions.md: what you did, why, what to avoid next time.

That's it. After a week, you'll have a decision log you never wrote.

Day 2 - Make Obsidian your prompt library:
Create ~/vault/03-docs/prompts/ and save your best prompts as Markdown files. Then tell Claude: "Your prompt patterns live in ~/vault/03-docs/prompts/, use them."

No more prompt graveyard in your notes app.

Day 3 - Close the loop:
Add a hook in Claude Code settings to auto-append session summaries to your inbox folder. Now your vault updates while you sleep.

You don't need 118 integrations. You need 3 files that talk to each other.


  
  
  The uncomfortable truth


We don't need smarter models. We need dumber storage.

ChatGPT has memory like a clingy ex - it remembers everything you wish it would forget and forgets what actually matters. Claude Code had no memory at all.

Obsidian fixed that. Not because it's smart, but because it's dumb in the right way. It's just text files on your SSD. You can read them. You can edit them. You can delete them.

The future of personal AI isn't a better chatbot. It's a vault that writes itself.

I stopped building a second brain. I started growing one. And it finally knows more about my codebase than I do.





Steal my exact stack?
I packaged the whole thing - the vault template with Memory Tree structure, all my CLAUDE.md files, the auto-sync hooks, and the 7 prompt patterns that actually write good docs - into a cloneable kit.

Get Obsidian + Claude Code: The Shared Memory Stack here: https://numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/obsidian-claude


P.S. It also includes the script that makes Claude write its own changelog, so you never have to write "what I did today" again.

title: Qlik Embed: The Replacement for Capability APIs That Still Isn’t Ready
title_hi: Qlik Embed: The Replacement for Capability APIs That Still Isn’t Ready
summary: I want qlik-embed to work. A simpler integration, modern authentication and less code to maintain should make moving awa
content:
I want qlik-embed to work. A simpler integration, modern authentication and less code to maintain should make moving away from the Capability APIs an easy decision.

I am using it now. OAuth integration was the deciding factor, with the push towards embedded AI adding another reason to switch. If I could have integrated OAuth as easily with the Capability APIs, I would have stayed with them without thinking twice.

Qlik calls it its primary embedding framework. For a straightforward chart, I can see why. For an application with extensions, maps, custom styling and its own error handling, the migration comes with compromises that are difficult to accept.


  
  
  Performance improved, until I needed iframes


My first attempts appeared to load the same scripts across multiple charts. The overhead was enough for me to shelve the switch. Performance has improved massively since then, and Qlik deserves credit for that.

But the improvement feels uneven once I need iframe="true".

Legacy extensions still take me back to iframe rendering through classic/chart. Qlik documents experimental preview="true" support for extensions and more chart types in analytics/chart. UI documentation

In my testing, that preview behaves as read-only. I cannot make selections, and it adds an unnecessary outline around the charts. I couldn't find either behaviour explained in the documentation. Broader chart support is of limited use when I lose the interaction that makes Qlik useful in the first place.

The iframe fallback brings back the performance cost I was trying to escape.


  
  
  Native charts should be the easy part


Maps are my clearest example. They are native Qlik charts, so I expected them to work through the modern chart component.

The current compatibility table explicitly excludes maps from standard analytics/chart support. Its classic/chart path requires an iframe. Qlik explains that tenant resources such as map tiles and uploaded images cannot currently be authenticated outside that mode. Chart compatibility

That helps explain the image failures I've encountered. It doesn't make the outcome any less frustrating. A native chart that needs tenant-hosted assets can send me straight back to the heavier rendering path. For maps, already expensive in my applications, that extra overhead has made the experience unusable in some cases.

Even branding can trigger the same compromise. Qlik documents that custom theme fonts need iframe mode when embedding across domains, with a possible performance impact. A font should not become an architectural decision. Custom theme documentation


  
  
  Less integration code, less control


With the Capability APIs, I controlled more of the chart lifecycle. During migration, reproducing my global error handling, custom loading states, chart error messages and authentication retries has been harder than it should be.

There is still API access. refApi exposes the embedded app for operations such as selections and bookmarks. My frustration is with controlling the surrounding experience consistently. refApi documentation

One recent example was trying to remove or restyle Qlik's interaction blocker inside an embedded extension. My React application could reach the outer container, but the cross-origin iframe prevented it from changing the internal element. Moving that styling into Qlik meant depending on internal selectors that Qlik itself warns are unsupported. Qlik's CSS guidance

A small visual adjustment had become a tenant-side workaround. That is the loss of control I mean.


  
  
  New features make the choice feel compulsory


Qlik Answers adds to the pressure. Its ready-made embedded experience is delivered through qlik-embed. It isn't something my existing Capability API integration simply gains. Assistant components

The documentation now labels ai/assistant as legacy and lists ai/agentic-assistant for the agentic experience. My rule with Qlik is simple. If it says legacy, I avoid it. In my experience, it brings more problems than it is worth.

The assistant still feels bolted on in my application. Getting it to match the surrounding typography, spacing and branding has been harder than I expected.

The Answers APIs provide another route for building my own interface. I appreciate having that option. It also means taking on more development to get the integrated experience I wanted from the component.


  
  
  There are reasons to keep going


OAuth is a welcome standard authentication route, even though I've encountered session problems with Cloud hubs and embedded applications open together in the same browser. Qlik's authentication guidance is also far ahead of what I had a decade ago.

A component with a few parameters is easier to start with than manually orchestrating visualization calls. Nebula.js and picasso.js give me another way to build charts with more control, if I have the patience or enough AI tokens to do the work. Nebula.js and picasso.js

I use qlik-embed because it gives me the OAuth integration and access to new AI components I need. I still need reliable maps, images and extensions, alongside enough control to make them feel part of my application. Until those everyday requirements stop pushing me into costly workarounds, I can't call it a complete replacement.

title: Show DEV: I built an AI/SaaS template with vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript
title_hi: Show DEV: I built an AI/SaaS template with vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript
summary: APEXVYRA is a front-end template for AI/SaaS products: a marketing site plus a full app dashboard, built with plain HTML
content:
APEXVYRA is a front-end template for AI/SaaS products: a marketing site plus a full app dashboard, built with plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. No framework, no build step, no backend.

I wanted something you can open in an editor and change directly, without first installing a toolchain or learning someone else's component abstractions.


  
  
  Why vanilla?


A few practical reasons:



Files you can edit directly. Every page is an HTML file. Change the markup, refresh the browser.

No build tooling. No bundler, no transpiler, no node_modules needed to run it.

Stack-agnostic. Because it's plain markup, CSS and small JS modules, it can be moved into whatever stack you pick later: server-rendered templates, a static site generator, or a framework.

Easy to inspect. View source shows exactly what's running. The JavaScript is split into small, single-purpose components (modal, tabs, tooltip, command palette, table sort, toast, sidebar, and so on).



  
  
  The dashboard


The app side is a 7-page dashboard:



Overview: KPI cards with sparklines and summary charts

AI Chat: a chat interface demo

Analytics: charts with legends and data-table views

Projects: project list/views

Team: members and roles

Settings: account and preference forms

Billing: plan and billing screens


All pages share the same sidebar and topbar layout, with the sidebar collapsing on smaller screens.


  
  
  SVG data visualizations


There's no charting library. The charts come from a small hand-written SVG renderer that supports:


line charts
area charts
(stacked) bar charts
donut charts
heatmaps
sparklines (in the KPI cards)


Each chart is an empty container with a data-av-chart-type attribute and a JSON config in a data attribute. A few things I cared about:



Theme-aware colors: resolved from CSS custom properties, not hardcoded hex values, so charts follow dark/light mode.

Responsive: SVG viewBox scaling, with axis labels thinned out on narrow screens.

Keyboard-accessible: data points, bars, segments and cells are focusable, with aria-labels and a shared tooltip on hover/focus.

Data-table fallback: every chart has a visible toggle to show the underlying data as a table.



  
  
  Dark/light mode and responsive layout


The theme is controlled by a data-theme attribute on the root element. A small inline script sets the initial theme before first paint to avoid a flash of the wrong theme, and a toggle component switches and remembers the choice. Colors are defined as CSS custom properties, so components and charts adapt automatically.

Layouts are responsive across desktop and mobile, including the dashboard's collapsible sidebar.


  
  
  What's included



24+ pages and screens (marketing pages, auth screens, blog, pricing, FAQ, legal pages and the 7-page dashboard)
30+ UI components
Documentation



  
  
  Live demo


👉 https://apexvyra-ai-saas-template.netlify.app

It's a paid template. If you're curious, the product page is here: https://marianemilian.gumroad.com/l/apexvyra-ai-saas-html-template

title: Why Digital News Has Become Part of Everyday Life
title_hi: Why Digital News Has Become Part of Everyday Life
summary: Digital news has become a normal part of everyday life. People who once relied mainly on newspapers and television can n
content:
Digital news has become a normal part of everyday life. People who once relied mainly on newspapers and television can now access information through websites, mobile applications, social media, and online video platforms.
The biggest change is convenience. Readers can search for information whenever they want instead of waiting for a particular broadcast or newspaper edition.
News at Your Fingertips
A smartphone can provide access to thousands of news stories within seconds. Whether someone is interested in business, technology, sports, entertainment, or world events, there are online sources covering almost every subject.
This accessibility is especially useful when an important event is developing quickly. People can check for updates without needing to wait until the evening news.
Online news has therefore changed not only where people get information but also how frequently they check it.
More Than Breaking News
Digital publications are not limited to breaking stories. Many websites also publish educational articles and background information that help readers understand complicated subjects.
For example, a technology story may explain how a new product works. A business article might provide context about a company's recent development. Similarly, an economic report may explain why a particular change could matter to consumers.
This additional context can make online news more useful than simply reading a headline.
Finding Reliable Information
The large amount of information available online also creates a challenge. Readers may encounter different claims about the same event, particularly on social media.
For this reason, it is useful to check the source of a story before sharing it. Readers should consider whether an article identifies its information clearly and whether the publication provides enough context.
Using several news sources can also provide a broader understanding of an event. Newsmax.it.com can be explored as an additional online source when readers want to discover news and information across different subjects.
The Role of Technology
Technology has made news consumption more interactive. Articles can now include photographs, videos, charts, interviews, and links to additional resources.
This allows readers to explore a subject instead of simply reading a short paragraph. Video reports can provide visual context, while links can lead readers to related information.
Mobile notifications have also changed the relationship between readers and news websites. Instead of actively checking a website every few hours, users can receive notifications when significant updates are published.
Social Media and News
Social media has become another important way people discover news. A story may first appear in someone's social feed before the reader visits the original website.
However, social media headlines are sometimes shortened or presented without enough context. Readers should therefore open the original article whenever possible.
Reading beyond the headline can prevent misunderstandings and give people a clearer picture of what actually happened.
What the Future May Look Like
Newsmax.it.com) The digital news industry will continue to change as technology develops. Artificial intelligence, personalized recommendations, short-form video, podcasts, and interactive content are already influencing the way information is presented.
The goal should remain the same: making useful information accessible while encouraging readers to think critically about what they see.
Conclusion
Digital news has made information faster and easier to access than ever before. From smartphones to computers, people can follow developments from almost anywhere.
At the same time, readers should remain careful about the sources they trust. Comparing information, checking dates, and reading complete articles are simple habits that can improve the online news experience.
As digital publishing continues to grow, responsible readers and useful news platforms will both play an important role in the future of online information.

title: How to Find and Replace Text Online Without Installing Software
title_hi: How to Find and Replace Text Online Without Installing Software
summary: When you need to update repeated words, phrases, URLs, or formatting inside a large block of text, editing every occurre
content:
When you need to update repeated words, phrases, URLs, or formatting inside a large block of text, editing every occurrence manually is slow and error-prone. A find-and-replace tool makes the job faster by locating matching text and replacing it consistently in one pass.


  
  
  Common use cases


Find and replace is useful for many everyday tasks:


Updating an old brand name across website copy
Replacing outdated URLs in a document
Correcting a repeated spelling mistake
Changing product codes or labels in bulk
Cleaning copied text before publishing



  
  
  A quick browser-based option


The Find and Replace Text Online tool from WebToolsEdge works directly in your browser, so there is no software to install. Paste your text, enter the word or phrase you want to find, provide the replacement, and apply the change.

A browser-based workflow is especially convenient for short editing jobs because you can review the updated text immediately and copy the result back into your document, CMS, email, or code editor.


  
  
  Tips for accurate replacements


Before replacing text in bulk, keep these checks in mind:



Use a specific search phrase. A broad term may match text you did not intend to change.

Review capitalization. Uppercase and lowercase variations may need separate replacements depending on the content.

Check the result before publishing. Read through the updated text to confirm the new wording fits every sentence.

Keep a copy of the original. For important documents, save the source text before making bulk edits.



  
  
  Final thought


Find and replace is a simple feature, but it can save a surprising amount of time when the same correction appears repeatedly. For quick, no-install editing, an online text replacement tool provides a practical way to clean and update content from any modern browser.

🌱 Touch Grass: TrailLens – Offline AI Nature Identifier

For Hacktoberfest 2026, I’m building TrailLens, an AI-powered tool that encourages people to spend more time outdoors by helping them identify plants and leaves while hiking, walking, or exploring nature.

📸 What it does


Take a photo of a plant or leaf outdoors
Use an open-weight AI model to identify it
Provide basic information about the identified plant
Designed to work locally, reducing the need to upload images to a remote server
Makes the screen useful for only a few seconds — then gets you back outside 🌿


🤖 Why open-source AI?

The open approach is an important part of this project. Using an open-weight model gives us the ability to:


Run AI locally
Keep personal photos on the user's device
Experiment with and modify the model
Swap models without being locked into one provider
Reduce dependence on paid cloud APIs
Potentially use the application in places with poor or no internet connectivity


This is where open innovation works better for this project than a closed, cloud-only approach: the AI can come to the trail instead of requiring the trail to have an internet connection.

🌍 Why “Touch Grass”?

AI shouldn't always keep us in front of a screen. I wanted to build something where technology is simply a bridge to the real world.

The goal is simple:

Take your phone → identify something → learn about it → put your phone away → explore. 🌱

Python
Computer Vision
Open-weight AI model
Local inference
Image Processing

title: BirdBuddy: an offline bird call identifier that runs entirely on your device
title_hi: BirdBuddy: an offline bird call identifier that runs entirely on your device
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass


  
  
  What I Built


BirdBud
content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass


  
  
  What I Built


BirdBuddy is an offline bird call identifier. You're on a trail with no signal, you hear a bird, you record three seconds, and BirdBuddy tells you what it is — with everything running locally on the device in your pocket.

The screen is the shortest part of the experience. Open the app, tap once, put the phone away. The identification finishes in about two seconds. No cloud round-trip, no account, no upload. Just you, the bird, and a 52 MB model that never leaves your machine.

Who it's for: hikers, birders, and anyone who's ever heard something beautiful in the woods and had no idea what it was.

Live demo: https://birdbuddy.onrender.com

Note: hosted on Render's free tier (512 MB RAM). The first request after idle may take 30–60 seconds to wake up. See the video below for the real, snappy experience.


  
  
  Demo


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7b3iXirhnTQ



What you're seeing:


The light, offline-first UI
Upload or record a 3-second bird call
Top-3 matches ranked by confidence
The top match spoken aloud by an on-device TTS voice
A Settings tab to tune Top-K, confidence threshold, and voice speed



  
  
  Code


GitHub: https://github.com/vinksgoyal/birdbuddy

Repo layout:



src/inference.py — BirdNET ONNX inference (audio → species)

src/voice.py — Piper TTS (text → speech, offline)

app.py — Gradio UI

scripts/tinker_finetune.py — Tinker fine-tune of Qwen3.5-4B for bird expertise

Dockerfile + render.yaml — one-click deployment

docs/ — Copilot usage screenshots



  
  
  How I Built It


BirdBuddy is built entirely on open-source AI. Three open pieces make it work.


  
  
  1. BirdNET v2.4 — open-weight acoustic classifier


BirdNET is a bioacoustics model released by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Chemnitz University. I used the FP32 truncated-DFT ONNX variant (~52 MB) running through ONNX Runtime on CPU. It classifies 3-second, 48 kHz audio into 6,522 species.

The model runs on a laptop, a phone, or a Raspberry Pi — no GPU required. Inference latency is under two seconds on a modern laptop CPU.


  
  
  2. Piper — open-weight text-to-speech


Piper is an MIT-licensed neural TTS that runs on CPU. I used the en_US-lessac-medium voice (~63 MB). When BirdNET returns its top match, Piper speaks it out loud: "I heard a Northern Cardinal."

No ElevenLabs, no Google Cloud TTS — the voice is a local ONNX model, just like the classifier.


  
  
  3. Qwen3.5-4B fine-tuned with Tinker


The audio model gives us a species ID. To make BirdBuddy useful and not just a label, I fine-tuned a small LLM to act as a bird expert — field notes, habitat, how to identify by sound.

I built a 165-example chat dataset covering 60 common North American species, then fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B with a LoRA adapter (r=16) using Thinking Machines' Tinker.

Training loss over 3 epochs:




Epoch
Avg loss




1
202.64


2
95.09


3
68.43




Baseline output on a held-out prompt (before fine-tune):


"I don't know how to use the API. ... Give me a field note for American Kestrel..."


Fine-tuned output (after training):


"American Kestrel (Falco sparverius) is a small falcon with brown upperparts and blue wings. Its shape, plumage, and behavior are useful clues when recording a field observation..."


That's the improvement the Tinker category asks for: a specific task, a clear baseline, a measurable gain.


  
  
  4. Built with GitHub Copilot


Copilot was the workbench for the entire project:



Copilot Chat in VS Code scaffolded src/inference.py, src/voice.py, and the Gradio UI

Copilot coding agent took Issue #2 and opened a PR that adds the GitHub Actions CI workflow

GitHub Actions now runs tests on every push









  
  
  5. Backboard R-CLI for dataset work


I used Backboard's R-CLI as a coding agent inside the repo for dataset curation and pipeline review — it summarized the inference pipeline, flagged missing error handling, and produced scripts/agent_review.md.


  
  
  Deployment


Docker + Render. The Dockerfile downloads both models (BirdNET and Piper) at build time so the container is fully self-contained. No API keys, no external services at runtime.


  
  
  Why Does Open Innovation Matter?


This project only exists because of open-source AI. Every design decision traces back to it.

The model is open-weight. BirdNET was released specifically for bioacoustics research. A closed API would have cost per call, required internet, and — critically — wouldn't have let me swap models. During development I tried three different classifiers. With a closed API, I'd be stuck with whatever the vendor offered.

The training data is open. The species library is a community-curated dataset of bird recordings. Thousands of birders contributed. A closed model trained on proprietary data would be a black box. I can inspect exactly what my model learned.

The runtime is open. ONNX Runtime means BirdBuddy runs on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS — even a Raspberry Pi. A closed inference service would lock me into one platform and one pricing tier.

The voice is open. Piper is MIT-licensed. Its voice models are open-weight. The TTS runs on the same laptop as the classifier.

The cost is zero. No API keys. No usage limits. No "your free tier has expired." A kid in a rural area with a hand-me-down phone can use this. A researcher in a country with unreliable internet can use this.

The agent harness is open. Backboard's R-CLI let me automate the boring parts — dataset cleaning, pipeline review — without locking my workflow into a proprietary IDE. I could inspect every step the agent took.

The fine-tune is open. Tinker let me fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B to a specific task and prove, with numbers, that the fine-tune beat the baseline. A closed model endpoint would not have given me the loss curve, the LoRA weights, or the freedom to swap base models.

The closed alternative would be: a subscription app that uploads your audio to a server, identifies birds you could have identified yourself, and charges $9.99/month. That's not innovation — that's rent-seeking.

This is innovation: a 52 MB classifier, a 63 MB voice model, a fine-tuned LoRA — all running on your device, in the middle of nowhere, for free, forever.


  
  
  My Agent Session


Backboard R-CLI session: sess_3f07cb2e — model openai/gpt-5.5, profile coding

The session covered:


Reading src/inference.py, app.py, and requirements.txt

Summarizing the pipeline
Flagging missing error handling on the audio loader
Producing scripts/agent_review.md




  
  
  Prize Categories


Entering:



Best Use of GitHub Copilot — Chat, coding agent PR, and Actions CI

Best Use of Tinker — fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B with a measurable loss improvement (202.64 → 68.43)

Best Use of Backboard — R-CLI agent session saved and embedded

Best Use of Render — deployed and live at birdbuddy.onrender.com



  
  
  What's Next



Package BirdBuddy as a real mobile app (React Native + ONNX Runtime Mobile)
Expand the Tinker fine-tune dataset to all 6,522 BirdNET species
Add a "trail log" that stores sightings locally and syncs later — never during the walk
Bring back a real hardware button on a Bluetooth clicker so you can record without touching the phone





Built with open-source AI, for the birds, and for everyone who'd rather be outside.

title: Building More Reliable Warehouse Robots: From Sensing to Verified Transfers
title_hi: Building More Reliable Warehouse Robots: From Sensing to Verified Transfers
summary: Warehouse robots can navigate between locations, but reliable material handling requires more than navigation. A robotic
content:
Warehouse robots can navigate between locations, but reliable material handling requires more than navigation. A robotic system also needs to determine what should be moved, where it should go, and whether the physical transfer actually succeeded.

In a dynamic warehouse, inventory information can be uncertain, aisles can become blocked, destinations can change, and pickup or handoff operations can fail. These conditions create an interesting engineering problem: how should AI systems connect perception, planning, execution, and verification?


Treat Material Identity as Part of the Decision


A robot may receive an instruction to move a specific load, but the available inventory information may not always be reliable.

RFID and UWB can provide identification and location context alongside robot perception. Instead of treating identification as a separate step, this information can become part of the planning process.

A system could consider questions such as:

What load does the robot believe it has identified?
How confident is that identification?
Does the available evidence match the assigned task?
Should the robot proceed or request intervention?

This makes uncertainty part of the decision process rather than assuming every input is correct.


Planning Must Handle Physical Changes


Warehouse conditions can change after a task has been assigned.

An aisle may become blocked. A destination may change. A robot may encounter an obstacle while transporting a load. A pickup can also fail before the planned movement begins.

A planning system therefore needs to account for changing physical conditions.

The challenge is not simply finding a route. The system also needs to maintain awareness of the load, destination, and task state as conditions change.


A Successful Command Is Not Always a Successful Transfer


A key distinction in physical robotics is the difference between command execution and physical outcome.

A robot can successfully execute a movement command without successfully completing the intended material transfer.

For example:

The robot may fail to pick up the intended material.
The handoff may not be completed.
The wrong material may reach the destination.
The destination may have changed during execution.

This creates a verification problem.

Instead of asking only whether the robot completed its assigned actions, the system should consider what evidence confirms that the intended material reached the correct destination.


Design Experiments Around Failure Cases


Controlled experiments can make these problems easier to study.

A mobile platform can move identified materials between stations while researchers introduce conditions such as blocked routes and failed pickup or handoff scenarios.

Performance can then be evaluated using metrics such as:

Delivery accuracy
Travel distance
Throughput
Congestion
Human interventions
Verified transfer completion

These measurements provide a broader view of system performance. A robot might achieve good travel efficiency while still requiring frequent intervention or failing to verify whether the correct material arrived.


Connect Perception, Planning, and Feedback


A useful way to think about the overall workflow is:

Identification → Perception → Planning → Execution → Verification → Feedback

RFID and UWB can provide identification context. Robot perception can provide information about the physical environment. Planning can use these inputs to assign loads, routes, and delivery tasks.

Execution moves the material, while verification determines whether the intended outcome occurred. Feedback can then inform subsequent decisions.

This is particularly relevant to Physical AI because the system's decisions ultimately affect physical objects and environments.


The Key Engineering Question


The interesting engineering question is not simply:

Can a robot move material from A to B?

It is:

What evidence should a robotic system require before considering a physical material transfer successful?

That question connects sensing, uncertainty, planning, execution, and verification. It also provides a way to evaluate warehouse robotics beyond navigation performance alone.

Aperture Venture Studio explores related scenarios involving distributed intelligence, robotics, material handling, and physical logistics through its research on distributed intelligence and physical logistics.

As warehouse environments become more dynamic, reliable robotic material handling may depend as much on knowing when not to trust an assumption as it does on navigating efficiently.

The goal is not just better movement, but better evidence for determining whether the physical task actually succeeded.
